title: Tail hedging: SLA vs cost snapshot (internal)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact internal snapshot of a small benchmark sweep we ran to quantify the cost vs SLA tradeoffs for several strategies intended to reduce tail latency (p99/p999) — what we're calling "tail hedging" options. The goal is practical guidance for product teams deciding which hedge to enable for a given SLA (p90 vs p99 target) and traffic mix.

Executive summary (short):
- Baseline (no hedging) gives the lowest $/q for steady workloads but exposes large p99 penalties under microbursts and cold-cache events.
- Model-variant hedging (route to faster, smaller quantized variant for strict tails) reduces p99 by ~30–40% at ~12–18% incremental cost relative to baseline.
- Prewarm pool (small warm fleet kept idle) cuts p99 by ~45–60% for high-frequency microbursts, but costs scale linearly with idle capacity and is best for predictable peak shapes.
- Polyfallback routing (probabilistic duplication to cheaper model + fast fallback) offers a middle ground: p99 reductions of ~25–35% for ~8–12% extra cost, with lower steady-state overhead vs prewarm.

Benchmark scope and constraints:
- Workload: synthetic mixed-conversation generator (50% short prompts, 35% medium, 15% long continuation). Injected microbursts: 200 qps -> 1800 qps for 30s at randomized intervals to simulate unpredictable spikes.
- Client profile: 95% single-turn, 5% multi-turn long sessions (KV cache hits vary).
- Models tested: M-large (baseline high-quality), M-small-int8 (fast quantized), M-medium (intermediate).
- Hardware: A100s for baseline and medium, 1/2 A100-equivalent for small-int8 variant (simulated faster throughput).
- Cost model: internal dollars-per-token proxy using runtime profiling + infra amortization. Reported $/100k requests normalized to baseline.
- Trials: 20 independent 30-minute runs per strategy; report median and interquartile where relevant.

Key numeric snapshot (median values across runs):

ASCII table: latency percentiles and relative cost

Strategy                      | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | p999 (ms) | Cost (rel) | $/100k req (norm)
------------------------------|----------|----------|----------|-----------|------------|-------------------
Baseline (M-large)            | 62       | 120      | 420      | 1200      | 1.00       | $100.0
Model-variant hedge (split)   | 68       | 125      | 270      | 720       | 1.15       | $115.0
Prewarm pool (10% idle cap)   | 60       | 110      | 200      | 520       | 1.45       | $145.0
Poly-fallback (prob 30%)      | 65       | 118      | 310      | 900       | 1.10       | $110.0
Small cold-buffer (burst srv) | 70       | 140      | 370      | 950       | 1.08       | $108.0

Observations on numbers: 
- Baseline p99 volatility is high: IQR of p99 across runs is ~+/- 160ms (unstable under bursts).
- Model-variant hedge increases p50 modestly (~+6ms) but dramatically tightens the long tail; best for teams wanting deterministic p99 improvements without large always-on cost.
- Prewarm yields the best tail improvement but at the highest steady-state cost (idle GPU hours). Worth it only when bursts are predictable or when SLA penalties are expensive.
- Poly-fallback is attractive when model quality can be traded probabilistically: background duplicates allow fast first pass and quality fallback. Works well if application tolerates occasional reruns or degrades gracefully.

ASCII visualization (very approximate): p99 over time for a representative microburst run (lower is better):
Time ->         00:00  00:30  01:00  01:30  02:00  02:30  03:00
Baseline p99(ms)    300   450    500    420    380    420    330
Model-variant       260   280    300    270    260    250    240
Prewarm             210   200    220    200    190    200    210
Poly-fallback       280   320    340    310    300    320    290

Cost dynamics notes:
- Prewarm cost ~ idle_gpu_hours * hourly_gpu_rate. If we hold 10% capacity to absorb spikes, cost scales with baseline fleet size. Example: for a fleet handling steady 500qps, 10% prewarm ~ 50qps capacity -> ~ 0.10 * baseline infra cost.
- Model-variant cost is primarily extra inference spent on duplicated requests routed to the faster variant; routing policy complexity adds small overhead.
- Poly-fallback cost depends on duplication probability and duplicate cancellation heuristics; with 30% prob and fast cancel we measure ~10% steady overhead.

When to choose each hedge (rough rule-of-thumb):
- Baseline: use when p99 is within customer SLA or when cost-sensitivity is dominant and spikes are rare.
- Model-variant hedge: good default for mid-tier SLAs (p99 target modest) — low infra churn, minimal ops complexity.
- Poly-fallback: for apps that can accept probabilistic quality varied by latency (search-like, suggestions).
- Prewarm pool: choose when consequences of p99 violations are high (monetary SLAs, churn risk) and burst patterns are predictable or frequent.

Open questions & follow-ups:
- Interaction with KV cache hit-rate: early runs assumed 60% session-level KV hit; we should re-run with 20% and 90% to quantify sensitivity.
- Cost model refinement: include network egress and shorter-term spot pricing variability (we used fixed-hour proxies).
- Quality regression check: model-variant hedging duplicates may introduce distributional skew — run evals with live prompts to ensure fallback doesn't change downstream metrics.
- Autoscale interplay: how aggressive autoscaling combined with prewarm affects queuing vs prewarm ROI.

Immediate recommendations (for product/infra owners):
1) For teams with p99-sensitive endpoints and moderate traffic, enable a conservative model-variant hedge (route 15–30% of requests opportunistically to small-int8 fallback). Monitor quality metrics for 2 weeks.
2) Reserve prewarm pools only for end-to-end payment/checkout flows or enterprise SLAs where p99 violation cost >> prewarm compute cost. Start with 5% idle cap and iterate.
3) Implement instrumentation: per-request lineage to track whether response came from hedge path, merge that flag into tenant-level SLO dashboards.

Appendix: short notes on methodology reproducibility:
- Repo: github:bench/tail-hedge-sweeps (see linked_artifacts)
- Run script: run_sweep.py --traffic-profile=mixed_conv --burst=1800 --burst_duration=30 --seed=42 --strategy=<strategy>
- Profiling hooks: runtime/p99_tracer.v2 (logs p50/p90/p99/p999 + cost-tag per request).

Notes to self: this doc is a snapshot for sync with product on Fri 10/18. Matteo to add KV-sensitivity runs; Jordan to add a brief note on UX-level acceptable QoS degradation.
